title: Instincts arise mainly by selection of accidental variations, not inherited habit

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Instincts arise mainly by selection of accidental variations, not inherited habit

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Complex instincts originate chiefly through natural selection preserving and accumulating slight accidental variations of instinct; the inherited effects of habit play only a subordinate role.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But I believe that the effects of habit are of quite subordinate importance to the effects of the natural selection of what may be called accidental variations of instincts

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VII, “Instinct”; section “Instincts comparable with habits, but different in their origin”. Scope: instinctive behaviour of animals in a state of nature

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch07-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.45

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern data can test genetic variation and inheritance for selected behaviours. They do not broadly quantify the historical balance between selection and inherited habit across complex instincts.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For instinctive behaviours with known pedigrees or genomic data, estimate heritable variation, selection, and transgenerational effects of acquired habits. Predominant response through heritable variants rather than inherited acquired behaviour supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Relative historical contributions are difficult to reconstruct.

Public behaviour datasets rarely combine pedigrees, selection, and transgenerational experiments.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Model-organism databases can reject a strong version of inherited habit for particular behaviors and can show genetic variation, which is part of the mechanism. They do not cover complex instincts in the wild, and they do not contain the selection history the claim puts first. The ranking 'chiefly' versus 'subordinate' therefore remains a proxy test on a small subset.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For complex instincts with genetic data, compare heritability and response to selection on breeding values with transmission of acquired habit in cross-fostering or training designs. A predominant genetic component and negligible inheritance of learned habit would support the ranking; inheritance of trained behavior comparable to selection on spontaneous variants would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No dataset ranks the contribution of habit against selection across instincts.

Showing that a behavior is genetic does not show that selection accumulated it historically.

Public genetic data are concentrated in a few laboratory species, not animals in a state of nature.
